meta.title: Word Bank
meta.note: One tagged bank for both halves of Paper 1. It merges the Continuous Writing handles in handles.json with new material this repo did not have: emotion ladders, phrases that work in almost any essay, and a register bank for Situational Writing. Nothing here is duplicated from handles.json; that file stays the single source for idioms, show-not-tell, strong verbs, openers, endings and transitions.
howToUse: Filter first, read second. Pick the feeling or the situation you are writing about, then read only what is left.
Take three items into a composition, not thirty. A bank is for choosing from, not for emptying.
Anything tagged Works anywhere is safe to carry into an exam without knowing the topic in advance.
For Situational Writing, set Paper to Situational and Register to Formal or Informal to match who you are writing to.

emotionLadders.note: Fear has two speeds. Sudden fear is a jolt, so use short words and short sentences: froze, flinched, terror. Slow fear is dread, which builds across a paragraph. Choosing the wrong speed is what makes a fear paragraph read as fake.
emotionLadders.sentence: Dread is the fear that arrives before anything happens; terror is the fear that arrives with it.

emotionLadders.note: Indignant is the most useful word on this ladder for PSLE, because it is anger at something unfair, which is what most school and family stories are actually about. Furious is common; indignant is precise.
emotionLadders.sentence: If your character is angry because something was unfair, the word is indignant, not angry.

emotionLadders.note: Devastated and heartbroken are for genuine loss, not for a lost pencil case. Using the top of the ladder for a small event is the commonest register mistake in P6 writing, and markers notice it immediately.
emotionLadders.sentence: Match the rung to the size of the loss, or the whole paragraph loses credibility.

emotionLadders.note: Joy is the hardest emotion to write without cliche, because over the moon and on cloud nine are the first things every candidate reaches for. Use one body action instead of one idiom and the paragraph immediately reads better.
emotionLadders.sentence: Write what the joy made the body do, and delete the word happy.

emotionLadders.note: Relief is a physical emptying, so it is best written as the body letting go: shoulders dropping, breath going out, hands unclenching. It is also the natural feeling for a falling-action paragraph, just after the climax.
emotionLadders.sentence: Relief goes downwards. Everything that was tight becomes loose.

emotionLadders.note: Guilt is about something you did. Shame is about who you feel you are. Regret is about wishing you had chosen differently. Most confession stories need guilt in the middle and relief at the end.
emotionLadders.sentence: Guilt is written in avoidance: the things the character will not look at and will not say.

emotionLadders.note: Shame is public and it lives in the face and the head: heat, redness, a head that will not lift. Mortified is the strongest single word a P6 candidate can use accurately and it is worth owning.
emotionLadders.sentence: Shame is felt in front of other people. If nobody is watching, the word you want is guilt.

emotionLadders.note: Embarrassment is smaller and lighter than shame and it usually passes within the scene. It is one of the few emotions that can be written with humour, which lifts a story.
emotionLadders.sentence: Embarrassment ends when the moment ends. Shame follows the character home.

emotionLadders.note: Quiet pride reads better than loud pride. A character who straightens up and says nothing is more convincing than one who announces how proud they are.
emotionLadders.sentence: Understate pride and the reader supplies the rest.

strong: unable to be glad for her
emotionLadders.note: Jealousy is best shown by a delay: the clap that comes a second late, the congratulation that arrives after everyone else's. The delay does the work that the word jealous cannot.
emotionLadders.sentence: Write jealousy as a small failure of timing, not as a declaration.

emotionLadders.note: Loneliness is written with distance and with objects: the empty seat beside, the phone with nothing on it, the group that closes as you approach. Naming it flattens it.
emotionLadders.sentence: Show the gap between the character and the group and the reader names the feeling for you.

emotionLadders.note: Crestfallen is a precise, marker-pleasing word that P6 candidates almost never use. It means the face falling at the moment the news lands, so it belongs in the sentence right after the result.
emotionLadders.sentence: Disappointment is the gap between what you expected and what arrived. Show the expectation first or there is no gap.

emotionLadders.note: Surprise is one beat long. Write it in one short sentence, then move to what the character does next. A whole paragraph of being surprised stalls the story.
emotionLadders.sentence: One sentence of surprise, then action.

emotionLadders.note: Worry is repetition. A character who checks the same thing twice is worried, and you never have to say so. Apprehensive is the exact word for worry about something that has not happened yet.
emotionLadders.sentence: Repetition is the grammar of worry.

emotionLadders.note: Determination is the value most PSLE prompts are secretly asking for. Show it as continuing after a specific failure, not as feeling motivated at the start.
emotionLadders.sentence: Determination only counts after something has gone wrong. Put the failure in first.

emotionLadders.note: Gratitude works best understated and shown by an action returned later in the story: the umbrella given back dry, the seat kept. Announcing gratitude in the last line is the weakest possible ending.
emotionLadders.sentence: Repay the kindness on the page and you never have to write the word thank you.

emotionLadders.note: Hope belongs at the very end of a story, and it should be cautious rather than certain. A guaranteed happy ending reads as childish; a small, uncertain, forward-looking action reads as mature.
emotionLadders.sentence: Cautious hope beats a guaranteed happy ending in every band.

emotionLadders.note: Regret is written in the conditional: what the character would have done. One would-have sentence at the end of a paragraph is enough; more than two becomes self-pity.
emotionLadders.sentence: Regret lives in the sentence beginning If I had.

emotionLadders.note: Exhaustion is written in the parts of the body that stop cooperating: legs that will not lift, eyes that will not focus, a hand that misses the handle. It also makes determination believable, so the two often sit in the same paragraph.
emotionLadders.sentence: Tired is a word. Exhaustion is a body that stops obeying.

universal.note: Phrases that fit almost any composition topic. Learn these and you walk into the exam already holding sentences, whatever the picture turns out to be. All of them are tagged Works anywhere.

items.phrase: By the time [X happened], [Y had already changed].
items.example: By the time the bell rang, the whole class had already decided whose fault it was.
items.why: Skips dead minutes and lands you in the next important moment.

items.phrase: It was not until [later] that [realisation].
items.example: It was not until I was on the bus that I understood what she had actually offered me.
items.why: Delays the understanding, which is exactly how real realisations work.

items.phrase: The next [hour / three days] passed in [one image].
items.example: The next three days passed in a blur of plasters, apologies and unopened homework.
items.why: Compresses a long stretch into one line without a boring summary.

items.phrase: For the rest of [the period], I [small repeated action].
items.example: For the rest of the lesson, I kept turning the eraser over in my fingers.
items.why: Shows a state of mind lasting, without naming the feeling.

items.phrase: Somewhere between [A] and [B], [the change happened].
items.example: Somewhere between the second lap and the third, I stopped counting and just ran.
items.why: Marks a turning point that had no single moment.

items.phrase: Two [weeks] later, [the thing was still true].
items.example: Two weeks later, the poster was still on the noticeboard, curling at one corner.
items.why: A clean jump for an ending or a falling-action paragraph.

items.phrase: I did not answer straight away.
items.example: I did not answer straight away. Outside, somebody was dribbling a ball against the wall.
items.why: A pause carries more weight than a described emotion.

items.phrase: Nobody said anything.
items.example: Nobody said anything. The fan turned twice.
items.why: Silence after a line of dialogue is the cheapest tension in writing.

items.phrase: That was when I [noticed / understood / stopped].
items.example: That was when I noticed the second bag under the bench.
items.why: Marks the exact sentence where the story turns.

items.phrase: Something in my chest [verb].
items.example: Something in my chest went tight and stayed tight.
items.why: A physical reaction that fits fear, guilt, worry or grief without naming any of them.

items.phrase: I heard myself say [words].
items.example: I heard myself say that I would do it, which surprised me more than it surprised her.
items.why: Shows a decision made before the character was ready, which is very human.

items.phrase: For a second I thought [wrong guess].
items.example: For a second I thought he was laughing at me.
items.why: Sets up a misunderstanding, which is the engine of most friendship stories.

items.phrase: That should have been the end of it.
items.example: That should have been the end of it. It was not.
items.why: Promises the reader that worse is coming, which pulls them into the next paragraph.

items.phrase: What I did not know was that [fact].
items.example: What I did not know was that the gate was locked from the outside at six.
items.why: Foreshadowing that is specific rather than vague, unlike Little did I know.

items.phrase: It was worse than I had thought.
items.example: It was worse than I had thought: the lid was off, and the tank was empty.
items.why: Followed by a colon and one concrete detail, this is a strong climax opener.

items.phrase: Then [the small thing that changes everything].
items.example: Then the lights in the corridor went out, one row at a time.
items.why: A one-word sentence opener that speeds the paragraph up.

items.phrase: There was no time to [sensible option].
items.example: There was no time to find a teacher.
items.why: Removes the easy solution so the character has to act, which the marker needs to see.

items.phrase: I had one [chance / minute / choice] left.
items.example: I had one attempt left and both hands were shaking.
items.why: Puts a countdown into the paragraph.

items.phrase: I could have [easy option]. I did not.
items.example: I could have walked past. I did not.
items.why: Two sentences that state the moral choice without preaching.

items.phrase: Before I could change my mind, I [action].
items.example: Before I could change my mind, I knocked.
items.why: Shows courage as speed, which is what courage actually looks like at fourteen.

items.phrase: It would have been easier to [X], and I nearly did.
items.example: It would have been easier to blame the wind, and I nearly did.
items.why: Admits the temptation, which makes the right choice worth marks.

items.phrase: One of us had to [act], and nobody else was moving.
items.example: One of us had to say something, and nobody else was moving.
items.why: Explains why this character and not another, which fixes weak plotting.

items.phrase: I made myself [action].
items.example: I made myself look at the screen.
items.why: Two words that convert an ordinary action into an act of will.

items.phrase: The [place] smelled of [two things].
items.example: The void deck smelled of drying laundry and yesterday's rain.
items.why: Smell is the sense candidates forget, so it is the fastest way to stand out.

items.phrase: Somewhere behind me, [a sound].
items.example: Somewhere behind me, a chair scraped.
items.why: Sound off the page makes a scene feel three-dimensional.

items.phrase: The [weather] had been [adjective] since [time].
items.example: The haze had been sitting over the estate since Tuesday.
items.why: Weather with a history, instead of weather announced in sentence one.

items.phrase: [Number] [objects] lay [where], [detail].
items.example: Three chairs lay on their sides, one still spinning.
items.why: A specific number plus one moving detail beats any general description.

items.phrase: It was the kind of [place] where [habitual thing].
items.example: It was the kind of canteen where the same four boys always had the same table.
items.why: Establishes a place and a social world in one sentence.

items.phrase: Everything looked exactly as it always did, which made it worse.
items.example: Everything looked exactly as it always did, which made it worse.
items.why: Ordinary settings around an extraordinary event are more unsettling than dramatic ones.

items.phrase: A small crowd had gathered without anyone deciding to.
items.example: A small crowd had gathered without anyone deciding to.
items.why: Crowds form by accident, and saying so sounds observed rather than invented.

items.phrase: Somebody at the back said [words].
items.example: Somebody at the back said it served him right.
items.why: An anonymous voice adds pressure without adding a character you have to manage.

items.phrase: Half the class turned round.
items.example: Half the class turned round before Mrs Lim had finished the sentence.
items.why: Measures attention, which is what embarrassment scenes need.

items.phrase: Nobody moved, and everybody was watching.
items.example: Nobody moved, and everybody was watching.
items.why: The exact social condition that makes a courageous act cost something.

items.phrase: The noise dropped, the way it does when [event].
items.example: The noise dropped, the way it does when a teacher stops in a doorway.
items.why: A shared experience the marker recognises immediately.

items.phrase: I told myself [reassurance], which was not true.
items.example: I told myself it was not my problem, which was not true.
items.why: Self-deception is the fastest way to make a narrator feel real.

items.phrase: Part of me wanted to [X]. The rest of me [Y].
items.example: Part of me wanted to run. The rest of me was already walking towards him.
items.why: Internal conflict in two sentences, which is exactly what Content marks reward.

items.phrase: I kept thinking about [small detail].
items.example: I kept thinking about the way she had folded the note into quarters.
items.why: Obsessing over one small detail is how guilt and grief actually behave.

items.phrase: If I said nothing, [consequence].
items.example: If I said nothing, Rahim would carry it for both of us.
items.why: States the stakes of silence, which sets up an honesty ending.

items.phrase: It had not occurred to me that [truth].
items.example: It had not occurred to me that she had been waiting all along.
items.why: A realisation that reframes the earlier paragraphs.

items.phrase: I still [small habit], and now I know why.
items.example: I still check the gate twice, and now I know why.
items.why: Change shown as a habit, not announced as a lesson.

items.phrase: We have not talked about it since. We do not need to.
items.example: We have not talked about it since. We do not need to.
items.why: Understated closure, which markers prefer to a summary of the moral.

items.phrase: [Object] is still [where it was]. [One thing has changed].
items.example: The kite is still on top of the cupboard. I have stopped promising to fix it.
items.why: Full-circle image with a single altered detail.

items.phrase: The next time it happened, I [did it differently].
items.example: The next time somebody sat alone at the far table, I did not wait to be asked.
items.why: Proves the change with a future action instead of claiming it.

items.phrase: I am not sure I would do it again. I am glad I did it once.
items.example: I am not sure I would do it again. I am glad I did it once.
items.why: Honest, slightly uncertain endings read older than triumphant ones.

situational.note: Situational Writing is 15 marks and is graded on Purpose, Audience and Context as well as language. The right phrase is the one that matches who you are writing to. Every function below gives you a formal version and an informal version; pick the column, not the sentence you happen to remember.

formats.label: Formal letter
formats.note: Dear Sir or Madam pairs with Yours faithfully. Dear Mr Tan pairs with Yours sincerely. Getting this pair wrong is a visible error on line one and line last.

formats.label: Formal email
formats.note: Same language as a formal letter, but add a clear subject line naming the purpose in under eight words.

formats.label: Email to a friend or relative
formats.note: Contractions are allowed and expected here. Writing it formally is as wrong as writing a principal's letter casually.

formats.label: Report
formats.note: Past tense, third person where possible, and facts before opinions. Headings are acceptable if the question allows them.

formats.label: Speech
formats.note: Address the audience directly at the start, use short sentences, and repeat the key phrase once near the end.

formats.label: Article or newsletter piece
formats.note: A hook first, then the information. Slightly warmer than a report, still not chatty.

functions.label: Saying why you are writing
formal: I am writing to enquire about [X].
I am writing on behalf of [group] regarding [X].
I am writing to request permission to [X].
I would like to bring to your attention [X].
informal: I thought I would write and tell you about [X].
I have got some news about [X].
functions.note: Say the purpose in the first sentence. Markers look for it there, and a warm-up sentence before it wastes a line you need for content points.

functions.label: Giving background
formal: As you may be aware, [fact].
The [event] took place on [date] at [place].
Our class has been [doing X] since [time].
informal: We have been [doing X] for a few weeks now.
functions.note: One or two sentences only. Background is context, not the content point.

functions.label: Asking for something
formal: I would be grateful if you could [X].
Would it be possible to [X]?
We should be most obliged if you would [X].
May I request that [X]?
functions.note: I would be grateful if you could is the single most useful formal sentence in the paper. It is polite, it is not begging, and it works for any request.

functions.label: Making a suggestion
formal: I would like to suggest that [X].
It may be worth considering [X].
One possible solution would be to [X].
Perhaps the school could consider [X].
functions.note: Suggestions score better when you add the reason in the same sentence: suggest X, so that Y.

functions.label: Giving a reason
formal: This is because [reason].
The main reason for this is that [reason].
This would allow [group] to [benefit].
Consequently, [result].
functions.note: Every content point is stronger with one because clause attached. It is the cheapest upgrade available in this paper.

functions.label: Raising a concern or complaining
formal: I am concerned that [X].
Unfortunately, [problem].
This has caused considerable inconvenience to [group].
I hope you will look into this matter.
informal: I am a bit worried about [X].
It has been a real nuisance.
functions.note: Formal complaints stay calm. Anger costs marks; the phrase considerable inconvenience does the work that exclamation marks cannot.

functions.label: Apologising
formal: I apologise for [X].
I am sorry for any inconvenience caused.
I regret that I am unable to [X].
informal: Sorry I could not make it.
functions.note: Apologise for the specific thing, then say what you will do about it. An apology with no follow-up action reads as empty.

functions.label: Thanking
formal: Thank you for [specific thing].
I am most grateful for your [help / time / consideration].
We greatly appreciate the support you have given.
informal: It was really kind of you to [X].
functions.note: Name the specific thing you are thanking them for. Thank you for everything is worth nothing.

functions.label: Offering help
formal: I would be happy to assist with [X].
Please let me know if I can be of any help.
I am willing to [X] should you require it.
informal: I can help with [X] if you like.
functions.note: Offers should be specific and bounded. I would be happy to assist with the setting up beats a vague offer to help.

functions.label: Inviting
formal: We would be delighted if you could join us for [event].
You are cordially invited to [event].
We hope you will be able to attend.
informal: Do you want to come to [event]?
It would not be the same without you.
functions.note: An invitation must carry date, time and place, or it loses content marks however well written it is.

functions.label: Turning something down
formal: Regrettably, I will not be able to [X].
I am afraid I have a prior commitment.
Much as I would like to, I am unable to [X].
informal: I do not think I can make it.
I have already got something on that day.
functions.note: Decline, give one short reason, then offer an alternative. Refusing without an alternative reads as rude in either register.

functions.label: Giving instructions or details
formal: Please note that [detail].
Participants are advised to [action].
Kindly [action] by [deadline].
The following items are required: [list].
functions.note: Instructions carry the underlined content point more often than any other function, so write them plainly and put each on its own line.

functions.label: Showing enthusiasm
formal: We are looking forward to [event] with great anticipation.
This is an excellent opportunity for [group].
I am confident that it will be a rewarding experience.
informal: It is going to be brilliant.
You are going to love it.
functions.note: Formal enthusiasm is measured. Excellent opportunity and rewarding experience carry it without sounding like a friend.

functions.label: Persuading
formal: I believe this would benefit [group] because [reason].
Not only would [X], it would also [Y].
I hope you will give this suggestion your consideration.
informal: It would make things so much easier for everyone.
functions.note: Persuasion in this paper is reason plus benefit to the reader's group, never pressure.

functions.label: Closing
formal: I look forward to hearing from you.
I look forward to your favourable reply.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
I hope you will consider my request.
informal: Say hello to your family for me.
functions.note: The closing line must match the purpose. If you asked for something, close by looking forward to a reply, not by saying goodbye.

functions.label: Sign-offs
formal: Yours faithfully, (only after Dear Sir or Madam)
Yours sincerely, (only after a named person)
Respectfully yours,
functions.note: Faithfully goes with a stranger, sincerely goes with a name. Memorise the pair; it is a free mark and a visible error when wrong.

functions.label: Opening a speech
formal: Good morning, Mrs Lim, teachers and fellow students.
Thank you for giving me the chance to speak today.
I am here to talk to you about [X].
functions.note: Address the audience in the order of seniority, then state the topic within two sentences. A speech that has not named its topic by sentence three has lost the audience and the marker.

functions.label: Closing a speech
formal: So the next time you [situation], remember [key idea].
Thank you for listening.
Let us all [call to action].
functions.note: Repeat your key phrase once in the last three sentences. Repetition is a speech technique, not a mistake.

functions.label: Report language
formal: The purpose of this report is to [X].
It was observed that [fact].
The majority of pupils indicated that [finding].
In conclusion, it is recommended that [action].
functions.note: Reports separate what happened from what should be done. Keep every opinion out of the middle and put the recommendation at the end.

registerPairs.note: The single fastest way to raise a Situational Writing mark is to swap the everyday word for the formal one. Learn these as pairs. In an informal letter, use the left column deliberately; in a formal one, use the right.

pairs.formal: I am writing to inform you

tagMaps.note: Tags for the material that already lives in handles.json, so nothing is copied twice. The Word Bank page loads handles.json, looks each item up here, and attaches the tags at runtime. f = feeling tags, s = situation tags.
